subject: Biology
unit: Unit I — Diversity of Living Organisms
title: Viruses & The Baltimore Classification System
topics: The 7 Baltimore Groups of Viral Genomes
quickSummary: Viruses are obligate intracellular nucleoprotein complexes containing DNA or RNA. The Baltimore classification categorizes viruses into 7 groups based on mRNA synthesis pathways. Bacteriophages follow lytic (virulent) or lysogenic (temperate prophage) cycles.

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary Box
summaryBox.takeaway: Viruses are acellular obligate intracellular parasites. Genomes are categorized into 7 Baltimore groups depending on how (+)mRNA is transcribed.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
VIRUS DISCOVERY MILESTONES
                            
  Dmitri Ivanowsky (1892)  ──► Filterable agent passes through porcelain bacteria filters
  M.W. Beijerinck (1898)   ──► "Contagium vivum fluidum" (Infectious living fluid)
  Wendell Stanley (1935)   ──► Crystallized Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV); proved protein nature
conceptBreakdown.content: Viruses are non-cellular, obligate intracellular parasites that lack metabolic machinery, ribosomes, and ATP-generating pathways. Outside host cells, they exist as inert crystalline nucleoprotein complexes (virions).

conceptBreakdown.heading: 9.1 Structural Architecture of Virions
conceptBreakdown.title: 9.1 Structural Architecture of Virions
conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
BACTERIOPHAGE STRUCTURAL ARCHITECTURE
                      
         ┌───────────┐
         │ Icosahedral│  <-- Head (Contains dsDNA)
         │   Head    │
         └─────┬─────┘
               │        <-- Collar / Neck
               │
            ======      <-- Contractile Sheath (Tail)
               │
           ┌───┴───┐    <-- Base Plate
          /  / | \  \   <-- Tail Fibers (Recognition/Attachment)
conceptBreakdown.content:
• Genetic Material: Contains EITHER DNA OR RNA, NEVER BOTH. Can be single-stranded (ss) or double-stranded (ds), linear or circular.
• Capsid: Protein coat surrounding the nucleic acid, built from repeating protein subunits called Capsomeres.
- Helical Symmetry: Capsomeres arranged in a hollow spiral cylinder (e.g., Tobacco Mosaic Virus - TMV; elongated rod $300\text{ nm} \times 18\text{ nm}$, contains ssRNA + 2130 capsomeres).
- Icosahedral Symmetry: Polyhedral shape with 20 triangular faces and 12 corners (e.g., Adenovirus, Poliovirus).
- Complex Symmetry: Binal symmetry containing an icosahedral head and a helical contractile tail assembly (e.g., T-even Bacteriophages T2, T4).
• Envelope: Lipid bilayer membrane surrounding the capsid in certain animal viruses (e.g., Influenza, HIV, SARS-CoV-2), studded with glycoprotein spikes (e.g., Hemagglutinin, Neuraminidase).

conceptBreakdown.heading: 9.2 The Baltimore Classification System
conceptBreakdown.title: 9.2 The Baltimore Classification System
conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
BALTIMORE VIRUS CLASSIFICATION
                                    │
    ┌──────────┬──────────┬─────────┴─────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
    ▼          ▼          ▼                   ▼          ▼          ▼          ▼
 Group I   Group II   Group III           Group IV    Group V    Group VI   Group VII
 (dsDNA)    (ssDNA)    (dsRNA)            ((+)ssRNA) ((-)ssRNA) (ssRNA-RT)  (dsDNA-RT)
conceptBreakdown.content:
| Baltimore Group | Genome Type | Pathway to mRNA Synthesis | Key Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Group I** | Double-Stranded DNA (dsDNA) | dsDNA $\rightarrow$ mRNA | Herpesvirus, Poxvirus, Adenovirus, T4 Phage |
| **Group II** | Single-Stranded DNA (ssDNA) | ssDNA $\rightarrow$ dsDNA $\rightarrow$ mRNA | Parvovirus B19, $\phi X174$ Phage |
| **Group III** | Double-Stranded RNA (dsRNA) | dsRNA $\rightarrow$ mRNA (via Viral RNA Polymerase) | Reovirus, Rotavirus |
| **Group IV** | Positive-Sense Single-Stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) | Genome functions directly as mRNA $\rightarrow$ polyprotein | Poliovirus, Hepatitis A & C, SARS-CoV-2 |
| **Group V** | Negative-Sense Single-Stranded RNA ((-)ssRNA) | (-)ssRNA $\xrightarrow{\text{Viral RNA Replicase}}$ (+)mRNA | Influenza, Rabies, Ebola, Measles |
| **Group VI** | Single-Stranded RNA with Reverse Transcriptase (ssRNA-RT) | ssRNA $\xrightarrow{\text{Reverse Transcriptase}}$ ssDNA $\rightarrow$ dsDNA $\xrightarrow{\text{Integration}}$ mRNA | Retroviruses (**HIV-1**, HTLV-1) |
| **Group VII** | Double-Stranded DNA with Reverse Transcriptase (dsDNA-RT) | dsDNA $\rightarrow$ RNA Intermediate $\xrightarrow{\text{Reverse Transcriptase}}$ dsDNA | Hepatitis B Virus (Hepadnavirus) |

conceptBreakdown.heading: 9.3 Viral Life Cycles: Lytic vs. Lysogenic Pathways
conceptBreakdown.title: 9.3 Viral Life Cycles: Lytic vs. Lysogenic Pathways
conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
LYTIC vs. LYSOGENIC CYCLES
                           
       ADSORPTION          Attaches to host surface receptors via tail fibers
           │
           ▼
       PENETRATION         Injects viral genome into host cytoplasm
           │
           ├─────────────────────────────────────────┐
           ▼                                         ▼
     LYTIC PATHWAY                           LYSOGENIC PATHWAY
     (Virulent Phage - T4)                   (Temperate Phage - Lambda λ)
     ├── Host DNA Degradation                ├── Integration into Host Chromosome
     ├── Viral Transcription & Translation   │   (Forms PROPHAGE)
     ├── Assembly of Virions                 ├── Replicates along with Host Cell
     └── Host Lysis & Virion Release         └── Induction via UV/Stress ──► Lytic
conceptBreakdown.content:
• Lytic Cycle (Virulent Phage - e.g., T4): Immediate host takeover, chromosome degradation, synthesis of viral capsomeres, packaging into mature virions, and lysozyme-driven host cell lysis.

• Lysogenic Cycle (Temperate Phage - e.g., Lambda λ): Phage DNA integrates into the host chromosome as a latent Prophage. Replicates passively with the bacterial host until environmental stressors (UV light) trigger excision into the lytic cascade.
